meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When they call the roll in the Senate, the Senators do not know whether to answer 'Present' or 'Not Guilty''?
meta.ogDescription: Not Roosevelt, or not first: the gibe was circulating in 1904 with no author's name on it. The earliest tie to TR is a biography published in 1923.

answer.label: Not Theodore Roosevelt — or at least, not first: an unsigned 1904 political joke
answer.authorDates: In print by April 1904 · no author named in any contemporary source
answer.sourceLine: This is a stock political wisecrack that was already circulating in April 1904 with nobody’s name attached, and the earliest version aimed at the U.S. Senate ran that September under the byline of a Minnesota congressman, J. Adam Bede, who aims it at the vice-president and does not credit it to Roosevelt. Nothing from Roosevelt’s own lifetime credits it to him; the first source to connect the two is a biography published in 1923, four years after his death, and even that reports it as a second-hand anecdote rather than a quotation.

source.heading: Where the joke actually shows up

docMeta.dd: Credited to Theodore Roosevelt everywhere, with no source ever given
J. Adam Bede, Congressman from Minnesota — the joke is aimed at the vice-president, not credited to Roosevelt
Lord Charnwood, Theodore Roosevelt (1923), p. 84 — four years after Roosevelt’s death, and as an anecdote rather than a quotation

source.excerpt: While his joys are few his sorrows are many, for how oppressive it must be to him in the light of recent events to look the Senators full and fair in the face and wonder as the roll is called whether they will answer “present” or “not guilty.” It can no longer be truthfully said that the Senate is a legislative body without convictions…
trail: 24 April 1904 — the joke is already loose, and it is not about the Senate. A San Jose Mercury News report has half the members of the New York legislature not knowing “whether they were expected to answer ‘present’ or ‘not guilty.’” No author is named. Cited by Barry Popik ↗

September 1904 — the earliest version pointed at the U.S. Senate runs in “Side-Stepping the Vice-Presidency” by Congressman J. Adam Bede, who imagines the vice-president wondering “as the roll is called whether they will answer ‘present’ or ‘not guilty.’” Bede names Roosevelt elsewhere in the article, but not in the joke, and never credits the line to him. Leslie’s Monthly Magazine, September 1904 ↗

1906–1907 — the gibe keeps circulating with no owner: a Cleveland Plain Dealer item of 3 April 1906 puts it in the mouth of an unnamed senator, and it turns up again in the Record of Christian Work that August and the Journal of the Switchmen’s Union in March 1907. All three citations are Popik’s ↗

1923 — Roosevelt finally enters the story, indirectly. Lord Charnwood’s biography reports that bodies which crossed Roosevelt “were accused of not knowing, when the roll of their grave assembly was called, whether to answer ‘present’ or ‘not guilty.’” It is an anecdote about his manner, with no date, no occasion and no quoted words. Charnwood, Theodore Roosevelt (1923), p. 84 ↗
source.excerptNote: “Him” is the vice-president, whom Bede has just finished describing as “the great American clam” — a man who presides over the Senate without belonging to it. Roosevelt appears nowhere in the passage.

source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording cannot be tied to any specific published work, so no rights status can honestly be asserted for the sentence itself. The two texts quoted on this page — Bede’s September 1904 article in Leslie’s Monthly Magazine and Charnwood’s Theodore Roosevelt (1923) — were both published well before 1931 and are in the public domain in the United States, but that status belongs to those texts, not to the line as it is usually quoted.

author.name: Theodore Roosevelt
author.kicker: The man it got pinned on
author.heading: Theodore Roosevelt
author.bio: Roosevelt is less the author of this line than the magnet that eventually collected it. He did have a documented habit of publicly ridiculing institutions that crossed him — his biographer Lord Charnwood wrote in 1923 of the comical vigor with which Roosevelt denounced “weighty personages and even august bodies,” and of the “Ananias Club” he kept for people he thought were lying. That reputation is exactly what makes an unsigned 1904 crack about crooked senators sound like something he would have said — which is how quotations end up attached to famous names.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented aimed at the U.S. Senate: J. Adam Bede, “Side-Stepping the Vice-Presidency,” Leslie’s Monthly Magazine 58, no. 5 (September 1904): 508 — which does not credit the line to Roosevelt. Barry Popik documents an earlier use of the same joke, about the New York legislature, in the San Jose Mercury News, 24 April 1904, p. 20. The earliest source linking the gibe to Roosevelt is Lord Charnwood, Theodore Roosevelt (Boston: Atlantic Monthly Press, 1923), 84.

misattribution.heading: Who has been credited, and why
misattribution.intro: This line is printed under Roosevelt’s name on essentially every quote-aggregator site, always without a source. The documented record points somewhere much vaguer.

items.why: Aggregators run the line under his name with nothing attached to it, and Wikiquote files it in its Disputed section ↗ with no citation of any kind. No source from Roosevelt’s own lifetime credits it to him.

By April 1906 the joke was being retold as a senator’s own rueful confession — a Cleveland Plain Dealer piece has an ex-congressman quoting a senator saying that when the roll is called in Congress he does not know whether to say “present” or “not guilty.” No name is given there either, per Barry Popik’s citation file ↗.

The earliest source that ties the gibe to Roosevelt at all is Charnwood’s 1923 biography — and it does not quote him. Page 84 ↗ says only that anecdotes abound of Roosevelt denouncing “weighty personages and even august bodies” who were “accused of not knowing, when the roll of their grave assembly was called, whether to answer ‘present’ or ‘not guilty.’” Note that it does not even say Senate.

misattribution.truthLine: The joke belongs to the muckraking politics of 1904, not to any one man: it was in print that April with nobody’s name on it, and the version aimed at the Senate ran that September over the byline of a Minnesota congressman who aims it at the vice-president and does not credit it to Roosevelt — the full citation trail is Barry Popik’s ↗.

context.heading: Why 1904 was the year for this joke
lead: The Senate the joke was written about was in genuine trouble. On 23 January 1904 a federal grand jury indicted Senator Joseph R. Burton of Kansas for taking money to intervene with the Post Office Department; he was found guilty that March and became the first United States senator convicted of a crime ↗ — a conviction the Supreme Court reversed on venue in January 1905, reimposed after a retrial that November and sustained on the second appeal — before he resigned his seat in June 1906. A gag about senators answering roll call with a plea was not an abstract insult that year.

And the man Congressman Bede pictured squirming was not Roosevelt but the vice-president, whom he had just spent a page describing as “the great American clam” — presiding over a body he is not a member of, with nothing to do but look the senators in the face. Bede then works the pun to its end: it can no longer be said, he writes, that the Senate is a legislative body without convictions. That is a joke built for a magazine column, and it reads nothing like a presidential aside.
context.detailsSummary: Why the line drifted to Roosevelt
detailsBody: Roosevelt is one of the most reliable destinations for an ownerless political epigram: he was president when the joke was circulating, he was famously blunt about corrupt officeholders, and he coined enough real insults that a borrowed one blends in. Charnwood’s 1923 biography shows the mechanism in action — he does not say Roosevelt coined the line, only that anecdotes abounded of Roosevelt accusing bodies that crossed him of not knowing whether to answer “present” or “not guilty.” A later compiler reading that sentence has everything needed to promote an anecdote into a quotation.
context.pull: It can no longer be truthfully said that the Senate is a legislative body without convictions.
